h1: Georgia HOA Lien and Foreclosure Threat Response Demand Letter
metaTitle: Georgia HOA Lien Foreclosure Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a Georgia HOA lien or foreclosure threat response demand letter. Protect your home rights under Georgia POA Act and challenge improper HOA liens.
statuteCitation: O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232 (Georgia Property Owners' Association Act, assessment lien) and O.C.G.A. § 44-3-109 (Georgia Condominium Act, assessment lien)
deadline: Foreclosure of the lien only by court action, not less than 30 days after certified-mail notice stating the amount due (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(c); § 44-3-109(c))
penalty: No foreclosure action unless the statutory notice has been given and the lien meets the statutory minimum; attorney's fees only where a statute or the covenants provide for them
introParagraph: If your Georgia HOA has filed a lien against your home or threatened foreclosure over unpaid assessments, you have important rights under state law. Georgia's Property Owners' Association Act (POAA) and broader condominium and lien statutes set strict requirements for how associations must notify owners, calculate amounts owed, and pursue collection. Many HOAs cut corners—adding improper fees, ignoring notice requirements, or threatening foreclosure without proper authority. A well-crafted demand letter citing the specific Georgia statutes can force your HOA to validate the debt, remove improper charges, or withdraw the lien entirely. This page explains how Georgia HOA lien law works and how a written response can protect your home before the dispute escalates to court or a non-judicial sale.
lawExplanation: Georgia HOA liens are governed primarily by the Georgia Property Owners' Association Act (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-220 through § 44-3-235) for communities that have formally submitted to the Act, and by the Georgia Condominium Act (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-70 et seq.) for condominiums. For HOAs not submitted to the POAA, only contract law and the recorded covenants govern—meaning many associations have far less lien power than they claim. Under O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(a), sums lawfully assessed by a properly submitted POAA association, including fines, are the owner's personal obligation and a lien on the lot from the time they become due, and recording the declaration is record notice of the lien. To the extent the instrument provides, the lien also includes a late charge not above the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the assessment, interest at no more than 10 percent per year, the costs of collection including reasonable attorney's fees actually incurred, and fair rental value (§ 44-3-232(b)). The lien may be foreclosed only by an action, judgment, and court order, not less than 30 days after notice is sent by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery stating the amount of the assessments then due and the authorized late charges and interest, and no foreclosure action is permitted unless the lien is at least $2,000; the lien lapses four years after the assessment first became due (§ 44-3-232(c)). Georgia's Senate Bill 406 changes that foreclosure notice and minimum-amount rule effective January 1, 2027. The Condominium Act has parallel provisions (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-109). Owners have defenses including improper notice, miscalculated balances, fines that exceed authority granted in the declaration, charges accrued during periods the HOA failed to maintain common areas, and selective enforcement. Under O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(d), an owner, mortgagee, or lender is entitled on written request to a statement of the assessments past due and unpaid, and an association that fails to furnish it within five business days loses the lien as to a purchaser or lender relying on the request.
letterStrategy: A Georgia HOA lien response letter works because it shifts the burden back to the association to prove every element of its claim. Start by demanding a full itemized accounting of all assessments, late fees, interest, and attorney's fees, citing your right under the POAA and the recorded declaration. Require the HOA to identify the specific recorded covenant or board resolution authorizing each charge. If you suspect the HOA has not formally submitted to the Property Owners' Association Act, demand proof of submission—without it, the association lacks statutory lien rights and must rely solely on contract remedies. Cite O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(c) (or § 44-3-109(c) for condominiums), which allows foreclosure only by court action after at least 30 days' certified-mail notice stating the amount due, and only if the lien meets the statutory minimum. Include a clear dispute of any improper fines, requesting copies of hearing notices and board minutes that imposed them. State that you reserve all rights under Georgia law including claims for slander of title and violations of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act if a third-party collector or attorney is involved. Set a firm 30-day deadline to respond, withdraw improper charges, or release the lien. A documented letter creates a paper trail that judges and juries find persuasive, often prompts the HOA's attorney to negotiate, and preserves your defenses if the matter proceeds to Superior Court or a foreclosure action.
proceduralNotes: HOA lien disputes in Georgia are typically heard in the Superior Court of the county where the property is located because they involve real property and equitable relief. Pure money disputes under $15,000 may be filed in Magistrate (small claims) Court, but liens and foreclosure cannot be removed there. Filing fees in Superior Court generally range from $200 to $230. The lien for an assessment lapses four years after the assessment first became due (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(c)), while a claim on the owner's personal obligation under a written declaration may be subject to the six-year period for simple written contracts (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-24). Always send your demand letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep proof.

faq.q: Can my Georgia HOA really foreclose on my home over unpaid dues?
faq.a: Yes, but only under specific conditions. For a property owners' association that has submitted to the Act, the lien may be foreclosed only by an action, judgment, and court order, not less than 30 days after certified-mail notice stating the amount due, and only if the lien is at least $2,000 (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(c); the Condominium Act is parallel at § 44-3-109(c)). Many associations threaten foreclosure they cannot legally execute, which is why a demand letter requiring proof of authority is often effective at stopping aggressive collection.

faq.q: What if my HOA never submitted to the Property Owners' Association Act?
faq.a: Many older Georgia HOAs were never formally submitted to the POAA. Submission requires a recorded declaration that specifically invokes O.C.G.A. § 44-3-220 et seq. Without submission, the HOA cannot claim the automatic statutory lien rights, expanded fee recovery, or other POAA protections—it must rely solely on contract terms in the recorded covenants. Demanding proof of submission is one of the most powerful early steps in disputing a Georgia HOA lien.

faq.q: Can I dispute fines that the HOA added to my lien?
faq.a: Yes. Under Georgia law, fines must be authorized by the recorded declaration, properly noticed, and imposed only after the owner receives notice and an opportunity to be heard. If the HOA cannot produce hearing notices, board minutes, or a covenant provision authorizing the fine amount, those charges can be challenged and removed. Improper fines lumped into a lien can sometimes invalidate the entire lien if not properly itemized.

faq.q: How long do I have to respond to an HOA lien notice in Georgia?
faq.a: While Georgia law does not set a single universal response deadline, most HOA pre-lien notices give owners 30 days to cure or dispute the balance. Before the association may foreclose, notice must be sent by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery at least 30 days earlier (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-232(c)). Acting quickly—ideally within 30 days—preserves your defenses, prevents additional fees, and maximizes leverage before the HOA's attorney files suit or records additional documents.

faq.q: Can I recover attorney's fees if the HOA's lien is wrongful?
faq.a: Possibly. If the covenants provide for prevailing-party attorney's fees, that clause typically works both ways. Claims such as slander of title may apply if the HOA recorded something it knew was improper, and attorney's fees may be available under O.C.G.A. § 13-6-11 if the owner specially pleads them and the HOA acted in bad faith, was stubbornly litigious, or caused unnecessary trouble and expense.
